Temptation Bundling
This concept comes from Katherine Milkman, Wharton professor of op-
erations and information management. She wanted to increase the
amount of exercise she was doing, but did not particularly enjoy going to
the gym. What she did enjoy was listening to audio books and she decided
to tie those two things together. At the time she was really into The Hun-
ger Games, so she decided only to allow herself to listen to it at the gym,
and guess what? She ended up making it to the gym five days per week
because that’s how much she wanted to hear the story.
   She called the process she used temptation bundling and decided to
test out the theory that “valuable healthy behaviors could be increased,
while guilt and wasted time from indulgent behaviors decreased, through
the use of temptation bundling” (Knowledge@Wharton, 2013). To test
out the theory, she recruited 226 students and faculty who stated that
they wanted to work out more. They were divided into three groups:

   ♠ Group 1 members were given iPods loaded with four tempting
       novels of their choice, but were only allowed to access them at
       the gym.
   ♠ Group 2 members received the same audio books but they were
       loaded onto their own iPods so they could take them home,
       although they were encouraged only to listen to the devices at the
       gym.
   ♠ Those in Group 3, a control group, were each given a $25 gift
       card and simply encouraged to work out more.

                                                   Beating Procrastination

   The findings were pretty impressive. Those in the gym-only audio book
access group (Group 1) attended the gym 51% more than the control
group (Group 3) and 29% more than the group encouraged to listen to
their personal iPods only at the gym (Group 2). Interestingly, the subjects
who rated themselves as the most crunched for time increased their gym
time the most using this method.
   You can use temptation bundling to your benefit by attaching things
you really like to activities that you dislike. Only drink your favorite bever-
age while studying, for example. Temptation bundling shows a lot of
promise and is at heart a reward strategy. Instead of punishing yourself
for doing things wrong, you reward yourself for doing things right!

Work in Short Bursts
Writing a dissertation is the kind of assignment that inspires procrastina-
tion at a very high level. When I was writing mine, I was also working a
full-time job. I heard about a book that advocated working on your dis-
sertation in 15-minute increments. I decided to give it a try. Each day I
would work on my dissertation for a minimum of 15 minutes no matter
what. On busy workdays, I might only complete a 15-minute task. Some
days, however, I would get in the groove and work for many hours. I
ended up finishing in a very reasonable time frame, and this solidified this
strategy for me.
    In the business world, David Allen, who authored Getting Things Done,
calls for a two-minute strategy. He says that if a task takes less than two
minutes, just do it and get it out of the way. Make the quick call, do the
quick chore, etc. The reason these ideas work so well is because they help
you to get over any barrier to starting. You are using action to create mo-
tivation. Also, objects that are in motion tend to stay in motion, so just
get started. Once you get started, the inertia can carry you through.
    Several poker players that I consult with have tried these methods and
they have found success. Taking 15 minutes a day to work on hand his-
tory reviews adds up over time. I also have clients who spend short bursts
of time learning new languages and even computer programming. No

Environmental Design
Sometimes you need to change your environment so that it becomes
much easier to do the things you want and avoid those you don’t. You can
make progress inevitable if you make some adjustments. To be sure, luck,
ability, timing, and strategy influence success, but moving forward can
become inevitable if you optimize your environment.
    We often procrastinate because we are in an environment that has too
many distractions. Don’t try to perform in an environment that’s distract-
ing – it is like rolling a rock uphill. Pychyl says that we need to minimize
distractions if we want to get things done; in today’s world, the internet
and social media are the top distracters. Pychyl found that 47% of the
time we spend online is purely procrastination. I offer a caveat to this
finding. Pychyl conducted his research before the advent of Facebook and
Twitter, so it’s safe to assume that today we spend more than 47% of our
time online procrastinating. Smart-phones are another major distraction.
If you want to get things done, you have got to reduce your temptations.
Pre-decide when you will take breaks and when you will work. Baumeister
and Tierney say that the essence of this strategy is to “lock yourself into a
virtuous path” (2011). The more we decide in advance what we intend to
accomplish and set up conditions to make that outcome more likely, the
greater the odds that our behaviors will match our intentions.
    Environmental design can include things like leaving your phone in a
different room. You don’t want to be interrupted when you are in flow by
any sort of notification. Intentionally eliminate options and distractions so
you can give attention to things that matter to you.
    You can also implement time simplicity, a process of simplifying your
time management. RescueTime (https://www.rescuetime.com/) is an app
for computers or mobile devices that tracks internet usage of apps and
websites for a week, then gives a report that breaks out how much time
the user wasted and where. Users can find out exactly which sites and

                                                  Beating Procrastination

apps are a time suck for them and take measures to limit their visits to

   If you want to take your environmental design to the next level, install
freedom (freedom.to) to block your access to your most distracting apps
and websites. There is a similar app for Mac users called SelfControl
(https://selfcontrolapp.com/). Take a look at the least productive web-
sites and use these apps to block them for whatever amount of time you
want.
   You can try other things like installing a newsfeed eradicator for Face-
book or temporarily removing icons from your desktop. The idea is to re-
move your top procrastination temptations so that you can consciously
choose where you direct your attention.

Simplify Your To-Do List
Another way to design for success is to ruthlessly eliminate tasks that are
not a good use of your time. Are there tasks and responsibilities you can
delegate? Consider using the Ivy Lee Method. Lee was a famous consult-
ant in the early 1900s who was hired to teach executives at Bethlehem
Steel task prioritization. He instructed each executive to take time at the
end of each workday to write down the six most important tasks for the
next day and put the list in order of importance. At the start of the next
workday he told executives only to work on the first task listed until it
was completed. Only then could they move to the second task, and so on.
Whatever didn’t get completed would get moved to the next day’s list
when the process was repeated. The result of carrying out this exercise
was that productivity went through the roof.
    There is also something known as Warren Buffett’s 25/5 rule. To do
this, write down the 25 things or goals that are most important to your
career development. Now circle the top 5. Buffett calls this your must-do
list. What happens to the rest of your list? Buffett allegedly called items
6–25 the “avoid at all costs list” because those items have the greatest
likelihood of derailing you and contributing to procrastination. It’s easy to
rationalize doing those things because they are at least somewhat impor-

Peak Poker Performance

tant to us, but they are not the highest priority. Buffett’s philosophy is
that we should only focus on the most important things – not the good
things – only great things! The fewer tasks you do, the more important
work you can get done. Also, do your most important tasks first thing in
the morning.
   Cass Sunstein from the University of Chicago developed an idea called
second-order decisions. These are rules we implement in our lives either
to avoid complex trade-offs or to remove the need to continuously reas-
sess everyday choices. Second-order decisions are a form of mental
short-cut, which can be either positive or negative. To use these to re-
duce procrastination, you can make daily rules like:

   ♠ I always watch 15 minutes of a poker video as soon as I wake up.
   ♠ I always go to the gym on Monday, Wednesday and Friday at
       10am.
   ♠ I eat vegetarian before 6pm.
   ♠ I do not eat candy until I’ve eaten a piece of fruit first.

   You can see that these little rules take willpower out of the equation.
Also, we don’t need motivation to adhere to our second-order rules – the
rule is just there – it’s what you do. It’s a pre-commitment or a pre-
decision. How you are going to behave has already been decided.

Create Accountability
Anthony Trollope was one of the most prolific authors during the 1800s,
a status he achieved primarily by using two main strategies: setting very
rigid writing goals and using an accountability strategy. He paid a man to
wake him every morning at 5:30am with coffee. As soon as he was up
with his coffee, he started writing.
    There are many ways to build accountability into your life. I’ve had cli-
ents start blogs where they write publicly about their goals. Some post in

                                                 Beating Procrastination

ments from your coach and agree on a due date. No matter the strategy

Summary
There is no doubt that the world offers many temptations and distrac-
tions that can take us off our A game. This chapter has offered a smor-
gasbord of ideas and suggestions to help you decrease the amount of
time you procrastinate on things you want to accomplish, but they are
just a starting point. Experiment with them; tweak them to make them
your own. If you can figure out your procrastination triggers and get rid
of them, you’ll be in fine shape to achieve more of your goals.

Chapter Highlights
   ♠ Procrastination is not rational.
   ♠ An aversive task, lots of freedom, no deadline, plus a touch of fear
       of failure makes for a perfect procrastination storm.
   ♠ Increase your expectancy and confidence, and you will decrease
       procrastination on average.
   ♠ Change the level of desire you have for a task, and your
       motivation will adjust accordingly.
   ♠ There are two types of procrastinators: the tense type and the
       relaxed type.
   ♠ Self-verification can drive procrastination.
   ♠ Don’t wait until you feel like tackling the aversive ask; just get
       started.
   ♠ Try some or all of the seven tactics to fight procrastination:
       implement intentions, gamify aversive tasks, bundle temptation,
       work in short bursts, design your environment, make tasks simple,
       or create accountability.

Peak Poker Performance

Jonathan’s Comments
Fortunately, procrastination has never been much of an issue for me. I am
quite good at motivating myself to get things done, likely because I real-
ize I am my own boss and that if I don’t work, I won’t make money, and
that if I don’t study hard, I will fall behind. Poker is incredibly competitive
and if you get lazy, you simply will not succeed. In order to be a successful
poker player you must be able to think very long term. For example,
spending time studying a specific abnormal situation that occurs infre-
quently may not pay off for years, but when it does, it will be well worth
the effort.
    However, I am not immune to procrastination. I tend to fall prey to
procrastination when I am in a long downswing. After losing for 15 or so
days in a row, I have a difficult time motivating myself to take a seat at
the poker table. During long losing streaks, I make a point to study more
than normal and to spend time doing things I enjoy, such as hiking, work-
ing out, reading books, and watching movies. My solution to this problem
is to take a few days away from poker and relax. After I am away from
poker for a while, I can return to the game with a new hunger. I suppose
this makes me a “relaxed procrastinator.”
    As noted at the start of the chapter when discussing Pychyl’s work:

      If you really want the perfect procrastination storm, put your-
      self in a situation where you face an aversive task and you
      have lots of freedom. Make sure there’s no deadline for good
      measure. If you add a touch of fear of failure on top, there’s a
      good chance you’ll never get anything done!

    This advice really hit home to me. Battling for significant amounts of
money is certainly an aversive task. You have the freedom to quit when-
ever you want. You don’t even have to play if you don’t feel like it. If you
fail, you lose your hard earned money. It seems like procrastination and
poker should go hand in hand.
    This is the exact situation most poker players are in. Those who have a

                                                 Beating Procrastination

decent amount of experience and success have enough money to live for
a few months set aside in their bank accounts. They don’t actually need to
make money in order to pay tomorrow’s bills so many players take time
off simply because they can. While taking time off is mandatory if you
want to stay sane, if you do it too often, you will quickly fall behind and
burn through your cash reserves.
     The main reason I have been so good at combating procrastination is
because I realize what must be done and do it. As Yoda says, “Do or do
not, there is no try.” When I accept a job or task, I simply must complete
it. I keep a detailed list in my phone of everything I need to do each day,
choose one task to be my main priority, and take care of it as soon as I
wake up. This ensures I almost always have a productive day.
     When I am playing poker the game is my main priority and I tailor my
schedule to accommodate playing well. This leads to me living as healthily
as possible and keeping distractions to the minimum. When I go to Las
Vegas every year for the WSOP, I realize I could have a great series, a
break-even series, or a horrible series. In my 10 years of playing the
WSOP, I have had a few great series, lots of break-even series, and two
horrible series. During those horrible series, I would show up at noon, play
for a few hours, lose an all-in coin confrontation, and then go home. I did
this over and over for the entire series.
     While some may think I’m crazy, I realize that as long as I’m playing
well, I will win some amount of equity each time I play. I did not go to the
WSOP to gamble and see what happens. I go to play every tournament
that makes sense. Before I arrive in Vegas, I know I will work hard for 45
days then go on a vacation after the series is over, win or lose. Having a
plan helps me to remain emotionally stable even when things are going
poorly. Many professional poker players have lost a huge amount of eq-
uity simply because they didn’t feel like playing. Don’t let procrastination
demolish your win rate.
